The Teacher Is a Direction, Not a Destination: Extrapolating RL-Induced Representation Residuals in On-Policy Distillation

Hao Li1,* MeiJia Chen2,* Weijie Ren3,* Donghan Li4
Zijun Tian4 Jingchun Huang4 Naibo Wang3,†
1University of Science and Technology of China 2Rutgers University 3Zhejiang University 4Independent Researcher haoli2101@mail.ustc.edu.cn mc2989@rutgers.edu 3200101501@zju.edu.cn mikeli1997qwe@gmail.com vaynetian@gmail.com jh2688@cornell.edu wangnaibo@zju.edu.cn *Equal contribution. †Corresponding author.
Abstract

On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student to match the teacher’s next-token distributions on the student’s own trajectories and has yielded substantial empirical gains. Generalized variants allow the student to surpass the teacher by extrapolating an implicit reward in output space. The language-model head, however, attenuates this change anisotropically: much of the change encoded in the teacher’s hidden states reaches the logits at a small fraction of its weight, and the sampled-token log-probability ratios on which output-space extrapolation relies inject noise that the extrapolation amplifies, making training unstable. We observe that reinforcement learning (RL) shifts a model’s internal representations relative to its base checkpoint, and that the direction of this shift can be measured at every layer. Motivated by this observation, we propose RIDE (RL-Induced Direction Extrapolation), which extrapolates the RL-induced change directly in representation space: at every layer and token position, RIDE computes the residual between the teacher and its pre-RL checkpoint and regresses the student’s hidden states toward targets displaced beyond the teacher along this residual. Conditioned on a sampled trajectory, this regression is equivalent to maximizing a linear directional reward defined by the residual under a quadratic penalty centered at the teacher, which makes explicit how the objective moves the student along the RL-induced direction while limiting its deviation from the teacher. Across four base/RL-teacher pairs spanning different scales, architectures, and pre-training lineages, RIDE approaches or exceeds the RL-trained teacher on every pair and is the only method whose mean does so, and it consistently outperforms output-space extrapolation, which degrades the student whenever the teacher is close to its base. Project page: https://github.com/xixixixixxxx/RIDE.

1 Introduction

Distillation transfers capability from a teacher to a student (Hinton et al., 2015), and on-policy distillation (OPD) has become a standard stage of language-model post-training (Yang et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2026). In OPD the student samples its own trajectories and receives per-token supervision from the teacher on the contexts it actually visits, which reduces exposure bias and provides a dense learning signal (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). A common use is to transfer the gains of a reinforcement-learning (RL) teacher to a student that shares its initialization, for example when merging domain experts or distilling an expensive RL run back into its base model (Xiao et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026b).

Standard OPD treats the teacher as the endpoint of learning, yet students need not stop there: the teacher-to-reference log-probability ratio acts as an implicit reward (Rafailov et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2025; Cui et al., 2025), up-weighting it relative to the KL constraint yields students that outperform the teacher (Yang et al., 2026b), and related methods extrapolate displacements in parameter or logit space (Li et al., 2026b; Zheng et al., 2025). Because RL updates are small, structured, and consistent across runs (Mukherjee et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Shenfeld et al., 2026), an RL-trained teacher supplies a direction as well as a destination, and a student that starts from the same checkpoint can continue along it.

Extrapolating in output space, however, measures this direction after the head has attenuated most of it. The language-model head reweights representation changes according to its anisotropic singular spectrum (Yang et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2026a): in Fig. 1, its 512512 weakest directions carry 79.8%79.8\% of the teacher-to-base residual’s hidden-state energy but only 30.0%30.0\% of its centered-logit energy, so output-space objectives supervise much of the residual only weakly and leave earlier layers unconstrained. The sampled-token log-ratio is moreover length-biased and prone to overoptimization (Park et al., 2024b; Rafailov et al., 2024), and scaling it by a global coefficient amplifies extreme rewards and destabilizes training (Yang et al., 2026b; Sun et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a). Hidden states retain the change before the head: feature-level distillation already uses them as supervision (Romero et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2020), its on-policy form OPRD matches student and teacher states layerwise with a deterministic per-rollout gradient (Yang et al., 2026a), and hidden-state directions encode behaviors that can be steered additively (Park et al., 2024a; Turner et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023; Arditi et al., 2024), which makes residual extrapolation a natural operation in this space.

We therefore propose RIDE (RL-Induced Direction Extrapolation). With the student initialized at the teacher’s pre-RL checkpoint, the three models share a representation space. On each student-generated context, RIDE evaluates the frozen teacher and the pre-RL checkpoint on identical tokens, takes their layerwise hidden-state difference as the RL-induced residual, places each target beyond the teacher along this residual with a single coefficient, and regresses the student’s hidden states toward it. Conditioned on a rollout, this regression maximizes a linear directional reward under a quadratic penalty around the teacher, and under a shared linear head the output-space extrapolation target of Yang et al. (2026b) is the head-projected image of the RIDE target; RIDE thus retains the reward-extrapolation view while replacing the sampled-token log-ratio with a deterministic hidden-state gradient.

On four base/RL-teacher pairs (R1-Distill-1.5B, Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Phi-4-mini), which span different scales, model families, and vocabularies, RIDE attains higher mean Avg@16 on AIME24, AIME25, and AIMO than OPRD and the output-space baselines on every pair and approaches or exceeds the RL-trained teacher itself, whereas output-space extrapolation falls below its teacher on every pair.

Our contributions are as follows.

  • •

    We identify the RL-induced representation residual, the layerwise difference between the teacher and its pre-RL checkpoint on identical on-policy contexts, as a measure of how RL changes the model’s computation. Both checkpoints are available in the same-initialization distillation setting.

  • •

    We propose RIDE, which extrapolates hidden-state targets along this residual with a single coefficient that recovers OPRD at λ=1\lambda=1, and we interpret the objective as reward maximization under a quadratic penalty, the representation-space counterpart of output-space reward extrapolation.

  • •

    We show that RIDE approaches or exceeds its RL-trained teacher on all four base/teacher pairs while consistently outperforming OPRD and output-space extrapolation, and we characterize its learning signal through analyses of head attenuation and conditional variance.

2 Related Work

On-policy distillation.

Unlike sequence-level imitation (Hinton et al., 2015; Kim & Rush, 2016), on-policy distillation samples from the student and supervises the prefixes it visits (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Ko et al., 2024); its sampled-token form is now a standard post-training stage (Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2026). Recent variants remove the need for teacher logits (Ye et al., 2025), reformulate the target for stability (Jang et al., 2026; Jin et al., 2026), analyze failure modes (Fu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026c), or use the model itself, given privileged information, as its own teacher (Zhao et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026). All of these approaches supervise outputs rather than intermediate states.

Learning beyond the teacher.

Viewing OPD as KL-constrained RL with an implicit log-ratio reward (Rafailov et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2025; Cui et al., 2025), generalized OPD up-weights this reward and obtains students that exceed the teacher (Yang et al., 2026b). A global coefficient, however, drives the student toward extreme reward peaks (Sun et al., 2026) and can collapse near-deterministic outputs (Li et al., 2026a), echoing the length bias and overoptimization of log-ratio rewards (Park et al., 2024b; Rafailov et al., 2024). Other methods extrapolate in parameter or logit space, either along a policy’s own RL trajectory (Li et al., 2026b) or along the difference between a fine-tuned model and its initialization (Ilharco et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2025). RIDE shares the premise that the RL-induced change is a usable direction, but measures it on hidden states, at every layer, before the head, and on the student’s own contexts.

Representation-level distillation.

Intermediate representations have long served as distillation targets (Romero et al., 2015; Zagoruyko & Komodakis, 2017; Tian et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020). OPRD applies layerwise hidden-state regression on policy, obtaining a deterministic per-rollout gradient and supervision that output-space losses cannot see through the head (Yang et al., 2026a); PHF instead matches the directions and geometry of hidden-state transitions (Li et al., 2026d). RIDE uses the residual from the pre-RL checkpoint to the teacher to place targets beyond the teacher, drawing on the approximately linear structure of behavioral directions in hidden space (Park et al., 2024a; Turner et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023; Arditi et al., 2024) and on the structured, consistent nature of RL updates (Mukherjee et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Shenfeld et al., 2026). Latent memory and internal-state interventions have also been studied in medical vision-language models (Zhu et al., 2026a; Zhu et al., 2026b).

3 Preliminaries

Notation.

Let πθ\pi_{\theta} be the trainable student and πT\pi_{T} the frozen teacher. Both are decoder-only transformers with LL layers, hidden dimension dd, a shared vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V}, and a language-model head Whead∈ℝ|𝒱|×dW_{\mathrm{head}}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d}. For a prompt x∼𝒟xx\sim\mathcal{D}_{x}, the student samples y^=(y^1,…,y^T)∼πθ(⋅∣x)\hat{y}=(\hat{y}_{1},\dots,\hat{y}_{T})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x). We evaluate all models on the same student-generated prefix (x,y^<t)(x,\hat{y}_{<t}) and write π(⋅∣x,y^<t)\pi(\cdot\mid x,\hat{y}_{<t}) for a model’s next-token distribution and hπ,t(l)∈ℝdh^{(l)}_{\pi,t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} for its layer-ll residual-stream state at position tt.

On-policy distillation.

Classical knowledge distillation trains the student on teacher outputs or teacher samples (Hinton et al., 2015; Kim & Rush, 2016). On-policy distillation (OPD) instead samples responses from the student and minimizes the reverse KL divergence to the teacher on the prefixes it visits (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024); by the chain rule of the KL divergence,

ℒOPD(θ)=𝔼x,y^∼πθ[∑t=1TDKL(πθ(⋅∣x,y^<t)∥πT(⋅∣x,y^<t))].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x,\;\hat{y}\sim\pi_{\theta}}\Big[\sum_{t=1}^{T}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,\hat{y}_{<t})\,\big\|\,\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x,\hat{y}_{<t})\big)\Big]. (1)

Estimating each local KL from the sampled token gives the commonly used tokenwise update

gOPDtoken​(θ)=𝔼x,y^∼πθ​[∑t=1Trt​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y^t∣x,y^<t)],rt=log⁡πθ​(y^t∣x,y^<t)πT​(y^t∣x,y^<t),g_{\mathrm{OPD}}^{\mathrm{token}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x,\;\hat{y}\sim\pi_{\theta}}\Big[\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(\hat{y}_{t}\mid x,\hat{y}_{<t})\Big],\qquad r_{t}=\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(\hat{y}_{t}\mid x,\hat{y}_{<t})}{\pi_{T}(\hat{y}_{t}\mid x,\hat{y}_{<t})}, (2)

in which −rt-r_{t} acts as a dense per-token advantage (Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025; Xiao et al., 2026). Relative to any reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, the same objective is KL-regularized RL with the implicit reward log⁡πT−log⁡πref\log\pi_{T}-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} (Rafailov et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2026b); output-space extrapolation scales this reward (Section A.1).

On-policy supervision as target matching.

Let sπ,ts_{\pi,t} be a model quantity at position tt, τt\tau_{t} its target, and ℓ\ell a discrepancy measure:

ℒ(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒟x,y^∼πθ(⋅∣x)[1T∑t=1Tℓ(sθ,t,sg(τt))],\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{x},\;\hat{y}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\Big[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell\big(s_{\theta,t},\;\mathrm{sg}(\tau_{t})\big)\Big], (3)

where sg\mathrm{sg} stops gradients through the target. Output-space teacher matching takes sπ,ts_{\pi,t} to be the next-token distribution and ℓ\ell the reverse KL divergence. Representation matching takes sπ,t=hπ,t(l)s_{\pi,t}=h^{(l)}_{\pi,t} over a set of layers l∈ℒlayerl\in\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{layer}} and over positions selected by a mask mt∈{0,1}m_{t}\in\{0,1\}, with the dimension-normalized squared error

ℓ⁡(hθ,t(l),τt(l))=1d​‖hθ,t(l)−τt(l)‖22,\ell\big(h^{(l)}_{\theta,t},\tau^{(l)}_{t}\big)=\frac{1}{d}\big\|h^{(l)}_{\theta,t}-\tau^{(l)}_{t}\big\|_{2}^{2}, (4)

which is on-policy feature distillation (Romero et al., 2015; Jiao et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2026a); conditioned on a rollout, its gradient is deterministic, unlike that of Eq. 2. Both instances set τt=sT,t\tau_{t}=s_{T,t}, so the teacher is the endpoint of learning.

Same-initialization setting.

We study a teacher obtained by RL from a base checkpoint, πT=RL⁡(πB)\pi_{T}=\mathrm{RL}(\pi_{B}), and a student initialized at that checkpoint, πθ0=πB\pi_{\theta_{0}}=\pi_{B}. This setting arises when an RL result is distilled back into its base model or when RL-trained experts that share a base are merged (Xiao et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026b). The three models share an architecture, a tokenizer, and a representational origin, so on a common prefix the difference sT,t−sB,ts_{T,t}-s_{B,t} measures what RL changed on that context: in output space it is the implicit reward log⁡πT−log⁡πB\log\pi_{T}-\log\pi_{B} (Rafailov et al., 2023); in representation space it is a vector at every layer, taken before the head.

4 Method

RIDE rests on the premise that an RL-trained teacher specifies a direction in addition to a destination: the teacher’s displacement from πB\pi_{B} is what RL contributed, and a student initialized at πB\pi_{B} can continue along it (Fig. 2). We state the construction in the target-regression template (Section 4.1), instantiate it on hidden states (Section 4.2), justify this choice of space (Section 4.3), and interpret the objective as reward maximization (Section 4.4; implementation in Appendix G).

4.1 From Teacher Matching to Residual Extrapolation

Within Eq. 3, teacher matching is the choice τt=sT,t\tau_{t}=s_{T,t}. We instead displace the target from the teacher along the RL-induced change:

τt​(λ)=sT,t+(λ−1)​(sT,t−sB,t)=λ​sT,t+(1−λ)​sB,t,λ≥0.\tau_{t}(\lambda)\;=\;s_{T,t}+(\lambda-1)\big(s_{T,t}-s_{B,t}\big)\;=\;\lambda\,s_{T,t}+(1-\lambda)\,s_{B,t},\qquad\lambda\geq 0. (5)

At λ=1\lambda=1 the target is the teacher and Eq. 3 is recovered; for λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1) it lies between base and teacher; for λ>1\lambda>1 it lies beyond the teacher, so the student continues the change that RL initiated. Because sT,t−sB,ts_{T,t}-s_{B,t} is recomputed for every rollout and prefix, the direction is not a fixed offset but the RL-induced change on the contexts the student visits. On log-probabilities, Eq. 5 yields the affine combination λ​log⁡πT+(1−λ)​log⁡πB\lambda\log\pi_{T}+(1-\lambda)\log\pi_{B} that underlies output-space reward extrapolation (Yang et al., 2026b). We argue below that this measures the displacement only after the head has attenuated most of it, and instead instantiate Eq. 5 on hidden states.

4.2 RL-Induced Representation Residual and the RIDE Objective

Given a student rollout, the frozen models πT\pi_{T} and πB\pi_{B} are evaluated on the same prefix (x,y^<t)(x,\hat{y}_{<t}), and the RL-induced residual at layer ll and position tt is Δt(l)=hT,t(l)−hB,t(l)\Delta^{(l)}_{t}=h^{(l)}_{T,t}-h^{(l)}_{B,t}. Because both models process the same tokens, Δt(l)\Delta^{(l)}_{t} isolates what RL changed in the processing of that context rather than the effect of a different trajectory; it lives in the student’s hidden-state space, is defined at every layer, and is computed deterministically from two forward passes rather than sampled.

Applying Eq. 5 to hidden states yields the RIDE target,

ht⋆(l)=hT,t(l)+(λ−1)​Δt(l)=λ​hT,t(l)+(1−λ)​hB,t(l),h^{\star(l)}_{t}\;=\;h^{(l)}_{T,t}+(\lambda-1)\,\Delta^{(l)}_{t}\;=\;\lambda\,h^{(l)}_{T,t}+(1-\lambda)\,h^{(l)}_{B,t}, (6)

and the training objective is the representation-space regression of Eq. 4 toward this target,

ℒλ​(θ)=𝔼x,y^∼πθ​[1|ℒlayer|​∑l∈ℒlayer1M​∑t=1Tmt​1d​‖hθ,t(l)−sg⁡(ht⋆(l))‖22],\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x,\;\hat{y}\sim\pi_{\theta}}\Big[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{layer}}|}\sum_{l\in\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{layer}}}\frac{1}{M}\sum_{t=1}^{T}m_{t}\,\frac{1}{d}\big\|h^{(l)}_{\theta,t}-\mathrm{sg}\big(h^{\star(l)}_{t}\big)\big\|_{2}^{2}\Big], (7)

where M=∑tmtM=\sum_{t}m_{t}. Unlike its log-probability counterpart, Eq. 6 involves no partition function. We supervise all LL layers and the final kk response positions, where student–teacher disagreement concentrates (Yang et al., 2026a). Only the target differs from representation matching, so λ=1\lambda=1 recovers OPRD exactly and any difference between the two methods is due solely to the residual term. Because Eq. 4 is unnormalized, the loss scale grows with λ\lambda; we keep this form so that λ=1\lambda=1 reduces exactly to OPRD and rescale the loss coefficient instead (Remark G.1).

4.3 Why the Displacement Should Be Measured in Hidden States

Two arguments favor hidden states over log-probabilities in Eq. 5: how much of the residual survives the head, and how estimation noise behaves when the target is displaced beyond the teacher.

The head attenuates the residual anisotropically.

Let h~\tilde{h} denote the representation fed to the head and z=Whead​h~z=W_{\mathrm{head}}\tilde{h} the logits. Since the head is linear, displacing its input along the residual displaces the logits along the corresponding logit residual,

Whead​(h~T+(λ−1)​Δ~)=zT+(λ−1)​(zT−zB)=λ​zT+(1−λ)​zB.W_{\mathrm{head}}\big(\tilde{h}_{T}+(\lambda-1)\tilde{\Delta}\big)=z_{T}+(\lambda-1)(z_{T}-z_{B})=\lambda z_{T}+(1-\lambda)z_{B}. (8)

Up to the log-partition constant removed by the softmax, the right-hand side is the log-probability target of Eq. 5; the output-space target is thus the image of the RIDE target under the head. The converse fails for two reasons. First, a logit target constrains h~\tilde{h} only weakly along the directions that WheadW_{\mathrm{head}} amplifies least, and Section 5.4 shows that the RL-induced residual concentrates in precisely these directions, so they reach an output-space loss at a small fraction of their weight. Second, a logit target imposes no constraint on layers below the final one, whereas Eq. 6 specifies the full vector at every supervised layer. Output-space reward extrapolation is therefore the head projection of representation extrapolation, which extrapolates the residual at full weight in every direction; the assumptions behind Eq. 8 and the head-drift term are discussed in Appendix E.

Extrapolation amplifies output-space noise but not hidden-state noise.

Fix a rollout and a position tt; write p=πθ(⋅∣x,y^<t)p=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,\hat{y}_{<t}), q=πT(⋅∣x,y^<t)q=\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x,\hat{y}_{<t}), and b=πB(⋅∣x,y^<t)b=\pi_{B}(\cdot\mid x,\hat{y}_{<t}), and let v∼pv\sim p be the sampled token. With ℓ⁡(v)=log⁡p⁡(v)−log⁡q⁡(v)\ell(v)=\log p(v)-\log q(v) and ρ⁡(v)=log⁡q⁡(v)−log⁡b⁡(v)\rho(v)=\log q(v)-\log b(v), output-space extrapolation uses the advantage Aλ​(v)=ℓ⁡(v)−(λ−1)​ρ​(v)A_{\lambda}(v)=\ell(v)-(\lambda-1)\rho(v) in the tokenwise update of Eq. 2 (Section A.1); both components are evaluated at a single sampled token.

Proposition 4.1 (Conditional variance under extrapolation).

Conditioned on the prefix, the variance of the output-space advantage over the sampled token satisfies

Varv∼p​[Aλ​(v)]=Varv∼p​[ℓ⁡(v)]+(λ−1)2​Varv∼p​[ρ⁡(v)]−2​(λ−1)​Covv∼p​[ℓ⁡(v),ρ⁡(v)].\mathrm{Var}_{v\sim p}\big[A_{\lambda}(v)\big]=\mathrm{Var}_{v\sim p}[\ell(v)]+(\lambda-1)^{2}\,\mathrm{Var}_{v\sim p}[\rho(v)]-2(\lambda-1)\,\mathrm{Cov}_{v\sim p}[\ell(v),\rho(v)]. (9)

The second term does not vanish as p→qp\to q unless log⁡q−log⁡b\log q-\log b is constant on the support of qq. Conditioned on the same prefix, the gradient of the RIDE objective in Eq. 7 is deterministic for every λ\lambda, so its conditional variance is zero.

The proof is in Appendix A. In output space the extrapolated component is a sampled estimate of ρ\rho whose noise is scaled by (λ−1)2(\lambda-1)^{2} however close the student is to the teacher, which accounts for the instability reported at large scaling factors (Yang et al., 2026b; Sun et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a); in hidden-state space the residual is computed rather than sampled, so λ\lambda changes only the destination.

4.4 Optimization Interpretation

The regression in Eq. 7 can be read as reward maximization under a proximity constraint. Fix a rollout, a supervised layer, and a position, and write h=hθ,t(l)h=h^{(l)}_{\theta,t}, hT=hT,t(l)h_{T}=h^{(l)}_{T,t}, and Δ=Δt(l)\Delta=\Delta^{(l)}_{t}.

Proposition 4.2 (Reward-and-penalty form).

Conditioned on the rollout, minimizing ℒλ\mathcal{L}_{\lambda} with respect to the student’s hidden state at each supervised layer and position is equivalent, up to a positive multiplicative factor and an additive constant, to maximizing

(λ−1)​r​(h)−12​‖h−hT‖22,(\lambda-1)\,r(h)\;-\;\tfrac{1}{2}\big\|h-h_{T}\big\|_{2}^{2}, (10)

where r⁡(h)=⟨h−hT,Δ⟩r(h)=\langle h-h_{T},\Delta\rangle. The maximizer is h⋆=hT+(λ−1)​Δh^{\star}=h_{T}+(\lambda-1)\Delta, and ∇hℒλ=2d​(h−h⋆)\nabla_{h}\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}=\tfrac{2}{d}(h-h^{\star}).

The reward rr is the inner product of the student’s displacement from the teacher with the RL-induced residual, the penalty is quadratic in the same displacement, and λ−1\lambda-1 weights one against the other; at λ=1\lambda=1 the reward weight vanishes and OPRD is recovered. This is the representation-space counterpart of the KL-constrained RL view of output-space extrapolation (Yang et al., 2026b); see Section A.3 for the derivation.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

Models.

We use four base/RL-teacher pairs; in each, the student is initialized from the base checkpoint (Section 3). The R1-Distill-1.5B pair consists of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and JustRL-DeepSeek-1.5B (Guo et al., 2025; He et al., 2025). The remaining teachers, Just-Qwen3-4B, Just-Llama-3.2-3B, and Just-Phi-4-mini, are obtained by applying the same RL recipe (He et al., 2025) to Qwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025), Llama-3.2-3B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and Phi-4-mini (Abouelenin et al., 2025). Within each pair, the base, teacher, and student share the architecture, tokenizer, and language-model head, which permits direct hidden-state comparison; across pairs, depth, width, vocabulary, and pre-training lineage all differ.

Training data and protocol.

Prompts are drawn from DAPO-Math-17K (Yu et al., 2025). Each method samples rollouts from its own current student policy, and the frozen teacher and, where needed, the base checkpoint are evaluated on those prefixes. All runs share the prompt dataset, sampling settings, optimizer schedule, and a budget of 500500 training steps. Unless stated otherwise, Sections 5.3, 5.4 and 5.5 use the R1-Distill-1.5B pair, and RIDE supervises all LL layers and the last k=2,000k=2{,}000 response positions with λ=1.25\lambda=1.25 and loss scaling by λ−2\lambda^{-2} (Remark G.1). Hyperparameters and hardware are listed in Appendix G.

Baselines.

We compare against sampled-token OPD (top-1) and top-16 OPD for output-space teacher matching (Agarwal et al., 2024; Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025); OPRD for representation-space matching, which coincides with RIDE at λ=1\lambda=1 (Yang et al., 2026a); and ExOPD for output-space extrapolation, which uses the same λ\lambda and pre-RL checkpoint (Yang et al., 2026b). The frozen teacher and the untouched student serve as reference points. Scaling coefficients are swept over the same grid as for RIDE. We omit weight-space extrapolation because ExOPD was stronger in the same setting (Zheng et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026b).

Evaluation.

We report Avg@16 on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and AIMO (AMC 2022–2023) (AI-MO, 2024a; OpenCompass, 2025; AI-MO, 2024b). For each training run, we average correctness over 1616 sampled responses per problem and then over problems within each benchmark; Avg. is the unweighted mean of the three benchmark scores. We use three independent training seeds (1414, 4242, and 20272027) for each trained method in Table 1, which reports the mean of the run-level scores. The teacher and untouched student are fixed-checkpoint reference evaluations, so their variation is not training-seed variation. Sampling and grading details are in Appendix G.

5.2 Main Results

Table 1 reports Avg@16 on the four base/RL-teacher pairs, Fig. 3 plots each method’s average relative to its teacher, and Table 4 reports the across-seed standard deviations for OPRD and RIDE. RIDE is the only method whose mean lies above the teacher line, on every pair, although on three pairs the margin is within one across-seed standard deviation (Table 4); all teacher-matching methods remain below the line, as their objectives dictate, and output-space extrapolation falls below it as well. Since RIDE differs from OPRD only in its target, its margin over OPRD (0.970.97 to 4.064.06 points) isolates the benefit of residual extrapolation under a shared protocol.

Figure 3 also separates the space in which extrapolation is performed from extrapolation itself: ExOPD and RIDE use the same λ\lambda and the same pre-RL reference and differ only in where the displacement is measured. ExOPD falls below its teacher on every pair, and on the R1-Distill pair it also falls below the output-space teacher-matching baselines (49.8749.87 versus 52.9052.90 for sampled-token OPD) even though RL moved this teacher 16.316.3 points from its base; on the three pairs where that change is small (2.82.8 to 6.06.0 points) it falls below the untouched student as well, by 14.114.1 points on Qwen3-4B. This is the behavior predicted by Proposition 4.1: the extrapolated component of the sampled advantage is scaled by (λ−1)2(\lambda-1)^{2} regardless of how much signal the log-ratio carries, and the damage is largest when the teacher-to-base gap is small. RIDE instead improves over the student and over OPRD on every pair, and over ExOPD by 9.19.1 points on average. On the Llama-3.2-3B pair the AIME benchmarks lie near the evaluation floor, so the evidence there rests mainly on AIMO.

5.3 Effect of the Extrapolation Coefficient

Figure 4 compares RIDE and ExOPD on the R1-Distill-1.5B pair for λ∈{0.5,0.75,1,1.25,1.5,2}\lambda\in\{0.5,0.75,1,1.25,1.5,2\}; at λ=1\lambda=1 they reduce to OPRD and to sampled-token OPD, so each row isolates extrapolation within one space. For RIDE, final Avg@16 rises with λ\lambda from 48.248.2 at λ=0.5\lambda=0.5 to 54.354.3 at 11 and peaks at 55.455.4 at 1.251.25; the neighboring coefficients λ=1.15\lambda=1.15 and 1.351.35 give 55.255.2 and 55.355.3, so every λ∈[1.15,1.35]\lambda\in[1.15,1.35] improves over OPRD (full numbers in Appendix B). Every run with 0.75≤λ≤1.350.75\leq\lambda\leq 1.35 improves steadily over the whole budget with a format score of 9494–97%97\%, and beyond λ=1.35\lambda=1.35 the degradation is graceful, with λ=1.5\lambda=1.5 and 22 finishing at 52.352.3 and 52.452.4. Displacing beyond the teacher (λ≥1\lambda\geq 1) shortens responses to 5.35.3–5.75.7k tokens, whereas displacing toward the base (λ<1\lambda<1) lengthens them to 6.86.8–7.47.4k. ExOPD is best at λ≤1\lambda\leq 1 (52.952.9 at 0.750.75 and at 11) and is harmed by every λ>1\lambda>1: the extrapolated runs reach their peak early (by step 150150 for λ=1.25\lambda=1.25 and 1.51.5) and then decline (λ=1.25\lambda=1.25 to 49.949.9, λ=2\lambda=2 to 46.246.2), the format score falls from 92%92\% at λ=0.5\lambda=0.5 to 64%64\% at 22, and responses lengthen to 8,7008{,}700 tokens. This is the behavior predicted by Proposition 4.1: the sampled-advantage noise scales with (λ−1)2(\lambda-1)^{2}, so the coefficient that moves RIDE further along the RL-induced direction moves ExOPD off the teacher’s formatting and below its teacher-matching baseline. Elsewhere we use λ=1.25\lambda=1.25 for both methods, the best value for RIDE and the smallest extrapolating value for ExOPD.

5.4 Mechanistic Analysis

Head attenuation reaches the learning signal.

The residual retains only 0.590.59 of the head gain of an equal-norm isotropic direction, and its energy concentrates in the weakest head directions (Fig. 5a); these directions receive 73.0%73.0\% of the representation-loss gradient but only 48.6%48.6\% of the output-KL gradient at the head input, so head attenuation weakens the output-space learning signal as well. The centered head is full rank, with singular values spanning 71.771.7 to 1.81.8, so the residual is attenuated by a factor of up to 4040 along its dominant directions rather than removed: an output-space objective still sees the RL-induced change, but at a fraction of its weight. The student’s update aligns with the residual (cosine 0.9540.954) and its head-visible component tracks the target (Fig. 5b, cosine 0.8950.895), with a projection onto the residual of 1.691.69, above the target coefficient of 1.251.25: λ\lambda specifies the target rather than the realized displacement, and the student continues past the target along the same direction. During RL the teacher head itself drifts from WBW_{B} by only 1.65%1.65\%, which supports the shared-head assumption behind Eq. 8; the representation-space target contains no head-drift term. Further measurements are in Appendix E.

The learning signal is deterministic in representation space.

At a fixed prefix, the sampled-token advantage of ExOPD varies with the next token, whereas the RIDE gradient does not (Proposition 4.1). On 9,1529{,}152 on-policy validation prefixes per method (Fig. 5c), the conditional variance of ExOPD rises 12.6×12.6\times from λ=1\lambda=1 to λ=2\lambda=2, with the extrapolation term dominating beyond λ≈1.3\lambda\approx 1.3, whereas resampling the next token leaves the RIDE per-position gradient norm unchanged at every prefix and every λ\lambda (drawn at the floor of the logarithmic axis). The decomposition of Eq. 9 also explains why ExOPD tolerates coefficients slightly above one: the covariance term is negative, so the variance has a shallow minimum near λ≈1.14\lambda\approx 1.14 before the (λ−1)2​Var​[ρ](\lambda-1)^{2}\,\mathrm{Var}[\rho] term takes over, which matches the sweep in Section 5.3, where ExOPD degrades at λ=1.25\lambda=1.25 and collapses at λ=2\lambda=2. The sampling protocol, variance decomposition, and uncertainty estimates are in Appendix F.

5.5 Ablation: The Residual Direction

A displaced target could help for reasons unrelated to the RL-induced residual, for instance by acting as a regularizer or by enlarging the loss scale. We therefore ablate the residual direction on the R1-Distill-1.5B pair with four controls that hold the displacement magnitude fixed and alter only its direction (Table 3 in Appendix C). The random control replaces Δt(l)\Delta^{(l)}_{t} with a Gaussian vector of the same norm; the reversed control uses λ<1\lambda<1, displacing the target toward πB\pi_{B}; the mismatched-origin control computes the residual against Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024), which shares the architecture but not the training lineage, so that hT−hB′h_{T}-h_{B^{\prime}} reflects a difference between unrelated models rather than the change produced by RL; and the trajectory-mismatched control computes hTh_{T} and hBh_{B} on separately generated trajectories rather than on the identical student prefix, testing the claim in Section 4.2 that the fixed context gives the residual its meaning. Relative to OPRD (54.5054.50), the random, reversed, mismatched-origin, and trajectory-mismatched controls reach 55.0455.04, 53.9053.90, 54.7554.75, and 55.1255.12, all within one point, whereas RIDE with the RL-induced residual reaches 56.3856.38.

6 Conclusion

An RL-trained teacher supplies a direction as well as a destination. The layerwise hidden-state difference between the teacher and its pre-RL checkpoint on identical prefixes measures what RL changed, and RIDE displaces the representation-matching target beyond the teacher along it; only the target changes, so λ=1\lambda=1 recovers OPRD. Measuring it before the head matters because the head attenuates the residual anisotropically and leaves earlier layers unconstrained, and because output-space extrapolation amplifies sampled-token noise by (λ−1)2(\lambda-1)^{2} whereas the RIDE gradient is deterministic given the rollout. Across four base/teacher pairs, RIDE approaches or exceeds its teacher, consistently outperforms OPRD and output-space extrapolation, remains stable where the latter collapses, and, as the direction controls show, owes its gain to the RL-induced residual itself. RIDE requires the pre-RL checkpoint and a shared representation space, uses a single global λ\lambda, and was evaluated only on mathematical reasoning with one RL recipe. Relaxing these constraints and studying the safety and calibration of students trained on hidden-state targets are left for future work.

Ethics statement

This work studies a training objective for distilling mathematical-reasoning ability from an RL-trained teacher into a student that shares its initialization. All experiments use publicly released model checkpoints and public prompt and evaluation sets (DAPO-Math-17K, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and the AIMO AMC 2022–2023 problems); no human subjects, personal data, or proprietary data are involved, and the task domain (competition mathematics) carries no direct risk of harm. Two considerations nonetheless apply. First, like any distillation method, RIDE transfers the teacher’s behavior, and therefore also any biases or errors that RL introduced into it, to the student; because RIDE displaces the target beyond the teacher, such properties could in principle be amplified rather than merely copied. Second, the student is supervised on hidden-state targets that no model has actually produced, so its calibration and safety behavior are not guaranteed to match those of the teacher and should be evaluated independently before deployment; we note this limitation in Section 6. We do not foresee misuse specific to this method beyond that of on-policy distillation in general, and we report the compute used (Table 5) so that the environmental cost of reproducing our results can be assessed.

Reproducibility statement

We have taken the following steps to make our results reproducible. The RIDE objective is fully specified by Eqs. 6 and 7 together with the loss rescaling in Remark G.1, and its implementation on top of an OPRD pipeline is described in Appendix G, including how the pre-RL checkpoint is hosted and how the target is formed and transmitted. Table 5 lists every training and evaluation hyperparameter shared by all methods (prompt set, rollout settings, optimizer, schedule, precision, hardware, supervised layers and positions, λ\lambda, evaluation temperature, and benchmark sizes), and Table 6 states the per-rollout cost of each method. All base checkpoints and the JustRL-DeepSeek-1.5B teacher are publicly available; the remaining teachers are obtained by applying the published JustRL recipe (He et al., 2025) to the corresponding public base models, as described in Section 5.1. Complete proofs of Propositions 4.1 and 4.2 and the derivation of the extrapolated advantage are given in Appendix A. The full extrapolation-coefficient sweep behind Fig. 4, including per-benchmark numbers, peak checkpoints, format scores, and response lengths, is tabulated in Table 2, and the sampling protocols and sample sizes for every diagnostic in Section 5.4 are specified in Appendices E and F. Training code, the RL-trained teacher checkpoints, and evaluation scripts will be released upon publication.

AI use statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools to assist with language polishing, checking consistency of terminology and notation, reviewing the presentation and interpretation of reported results, and verifying bibliographic metadata against source records. The tools did not design or run experiments or generate the reported measurements, figures, or tables. The authors are responsible for the research decisions, technical claims, and final manuscript, including AI-assisted edits.

Appendix A Derivations and Proofs

A.1 On-Policy Distillation as Implicit-Reward Reinforcement Learning

Fix a prefix and write p=πθ(⋅∣x,y^<t)p=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,\hat{y}_{<t}), q=πT(⋅∣x,y^<t)q=\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x,\hat{y}_{<t}), and let πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} be any reference policy with full support. Adding and subtracting log⁡πref\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} inside the local KL of Eq. 1 gives

DKL(p∥q)=DKL(p∥πref)−𝔼v∼p[logq(v)−logπref(v)],D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\,\|\,q)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})-\mathbb{E}_{v\sim p}\big[\log q(v)-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(v)\big], (11)

so minimizing the OPD loss is KL-regularized RL with the implicit reward log⁡q−log⁡πref\log q-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, in which the reward and the KL term have equal weight (Yang et al., 2026b). Weighting the reward by λ\lambda instead, the local objective λ𝔼v∼p[logq−logπref]−DKL(p∥πref)\lambda\,\mathbb{E}_{v\sim p}[\log q-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}]-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) is maximized by

log⁡p⋆=λ​log⁡q+(1−λ)​log⁡πref−log⁡Z,\log p^{\star}=\lambda\log q+(1-\lambda)\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}-\log Z, (12)

where ZZ normalizes p⋆p^{\star}. With πref=πB\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}=\pi_{B} this is Eq. 5 on log-probabilities. Minimizing DKL(p∥p⋆)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\,\|\,p^{\star}) with the sampled-token estimator of Eq. 2 uses the per-token quantity

log⁡p⁡(v)−log⁡p⋆​(v)=ℓ⁡(v)−(λ−1)​ρ​(v)+log⁡Z,\log p(v)-\log p^{\star}(v)=\ell(v)-(\lambda-1)\rho(v)+\log Z, (13)

with ℓ\ell and ρ\rho as in Section 4.3. The constant log⁡Z\log Z does not depend on vv and multiplies a score function with zero conditional mean, so the extrapolated advantage is Aλ​(v)=ℓ⁡(v)−(λ−1)​ρ​(v)A_{\lambda}(v)=\ell(v)-(\lambda-1)\rho(v). The tokenwise update treats sampled prefixes as fixed; differentiating the sequence-level objective in Eq. 1 would additionally account for how earlier actions change later prefixes.

A.2 Proof of Proposition 4.1

For random variables X,YX,Y and a constant cc, Var⁡[X−c​Y]=Var⁡[X]+c2​Var​[Y]−2​c​Cov​[X,Y]\mathrm{Var}[X-cY]=\mathrm{Var}[X]+c^{2}\mathrm{Var}[Y]-2c\,\mathrm{Cov}[X,Y]. Taking X=ℓ⁡(v)X=\ell(v), Y=ρ⁡(v)Y=\rho(v), c=λ−1c=\lambda-1, and v∼pv\sim p gives Eq. 9. Since qq and bb are frozen, ρ\rho does not depend on θ\theta, and the second term grows quadratically in λ−1\lambda-1. As p→qp\to q, Varv∼p​[ρ⁡(v)]→Varv∼q​[ρ⁡(v)]\mathrm{Var}_{v\sim p}[\rho(v)]\to\mathrm{Var}_{v\sim q}[\rho(v)], which vanishes only if log⁡q−log⁡b\log q-\log b is constant on the support of qq, that is, only if RL left the next-token distribution at this prefix unchanged.

For RIDE, the student state hθ,t(l)h^{(l)}_{\theta,t} is a deterministic function of θ\theta and the prefix, and the target ht⋆(l)h^{\star(l)}_{t} is a deterministic function of the prefix and the two frozen models. Neither depends on the token sampled at position tt, so the per-position loss and its gradient with respect to θ\theta are invariant to resampling that token, and their conditional variance is zero.

A.3 Reward-and-Penalty Form: Derivation of Proposition 4.2

With hh, hTh_{T}, and Δ\Delta as in Section 4.4, expanding the squared distance to the target gives

‖h−hT−(λ−1)​Δ‖22=‖h−hT‖22−2​(λ−1)​⟨h−hT,Δ⟩+(λ−1)2​‖Δ‖22,\big\|h-h_{T}-(\lambda-1)\Delta\big\|_{2}^{2}=\big\|h-h_{T}\big\|_{2}^{2}-2(\lambda-1)\big\langle h-h_{T},\;\Delta\big\rangle+(\lambda-1)^{2}\|\Delta\|_{2}^{2}, (14)

in which the final term is independent of θ\theta. The squared distance therefore equals ‖h−hT‖22−2​(λ−1)​r​(h)\|h-h_{T}\|_{2}^{2}-2(\lambda-1)\,r(h) plus a constant, and multiplying by −12-\tfrac{1}{2} gives Eq. 10 up to an additive constant; the per-position loss is this squared distance scaled by the positive factor 1/d1/d. The objective in Eq. 10 is strictly concave in hh with gradient (λ−1)​Δ−(h−hT)(\lambda-1)\Delta-(h-h_{T}), which vanishes at h⋆=hT+(λ−1)​Δh^{\star}=h_{T}+(\lambda-1)\Delta. Differentiating 1d​‖h−h⋆‖22\tfrac{1}{d}\|h-h^{\star}\|_{2}^{2} gives 2d​(h−h⋆)\tfrac{2}{d}(h-h^{\star}).

The reward rr measures the extent to which the student’s displacement from the teacher is aligned with the RL-induced residual, the penalty is quadratic in the same displacement, and λ−1\lambda-1 weights the reward against the penalty. This mirrors the view of output-space extrapolation as KL-constrained RL around the teacher (Yang et al., 2026b), with the KL constraint replaced by a quadratic one, the log-ratio reward by an inner product with the residual, and the score-function estimator by a vector gradient. At λ=1\lambda=1 the reward weight vanishes: teacher matching is a special case of RIDE rather than its point of departure.

Table 2 lists the numbers behind Fig. 4: validation Avg@16 on AIME24, AIME25, and AIMO at the final checkpoint, the validation format score, and the mean training response length over the 5050 steps preceding the final checkpoint. The two additional RIDE coefficients λ=1.15\lambda=1.15 and 1.351.35 are included; they bracket λ=1.25\lambda=1.25 and both remain above OPRD (55.255.2 and 55.355.3 versus 54.354.3), so every coefficient in [1.15,1.35][1.15,1.35] improves over teacher matching, with λ=1.25\lambda=1.25 the best. The sweep uses a single training seed per coefficient, whereas Table 1 averages three seeds; the λ=1\lambda=1 and λ=1.25\lambda=1.25 rows of Table 2 are therefore single runs (54.354.3 and 55.455.4) and differ from the corresponding three-seed means in Table 1 (54.5054.50 and 56.3856.38) by about one across-seed standard deviation (Table 4). Figure 6 shows the final Avg@16 on each benchmark as a function of λ\lambda: the gain of RIDE around λ=1.25\lambda=1.25 and the decline of ExOPD beyond λ=1\lambda=1 appear on all three benchmarks, not only in the macro average. Figure 7a places every run in the length–accuracy plane; increasing λ\lambda moves RIDE toward shorter and more accurate responses with a high format score, whereas it moves ExOPD toward longer and less accurate ones. Figure 7b summarizes the last 200200 training steps of each run in Fig. 4 by the mean and the min–max range of validation Avg@16 over steps 300300–500500. For RIDE, the late-training mean rises from 54.354.3 at λ=1\lambda=1 to 54.754.7 at λ=1.25\lambda=1.25, and every run with λ≥0.75\lambda\geq 0.75 stays above 50.950.9 throughout the window; for ExOPD, the late-training mean of every λ>1\lambda>1 run lies below that of λ=1\lambda=1 (53.653.6), the ranges widen to 3.23.2–5.15.1 points, and the λ=2\lambda=2 run drifts from 51.251.2 to 46.246.2 within the window, so the coefficient that improves RIDE degrades ExOPD and makes its late-training behavior less stable. For RIDE, every λ≥1.15\lambda\geq 1.15 shortens responses relative to OPRD while λ≤0.75\lambda\leq 0.75 lengthens them; for ExOPD, the final Avg@16 is non-monotone in λ\lambda and every λ>1\lambda>1 ends below the λ=1\lambda=1 run, and the format score decreases with λ\lambda except for a partial recovery at λ=1.5\lambda=1.5.

Appendix E Additional Head Diagnostics

The measurements in Fig. 5 use 292,864292{,}864 positions from the R1-Distill-1.5B pair: 143143 problems, 1616 rollouts each, and 128128 positions per rollout from the last 2,0002{,}000 response tokens at step 500500. The residual’s normalized head gain is 0.590.59 (prompt-bootstrap 95%95\% CI [0.585,0.596][0.585,0.596]), and its hidden-state energy outside the top-rr head subspace exceeds the isotropic expectation at every rr. The centered head is full rank, with singular values ranging from 71.7071.70 to 1.781.78, so the residual is attenuated rather than removed. Across training steps, the 512512 weakest directions carry 73.00%73.00\% of the representation-loss gradient of Eq. 7, versus 48.60%48.60\% of the output-KL gradient at the head input.

Scope of Eq. 8.

Equation 7 supervises the pre-normalization residual stream, so Eq. 8 holds after the final normalization is applied to the target; the identity is stated at the head input so that it holds exactly. It also assumes the head shared by base and student: a teacher whose head drifted during RL contributes an additional term (WT−WB)​h~T(W_{T}-W_{B})\tilde{h}_{T} to its native output-space target, quantified below. With WBW_{B} fixed, the head image of the RIDE target matches λ​zT+(1−λ)​zB\lambda z_{T}+(1-\lambda)z_{B} to relative error 6.50×10−76.50\times 10^{-7}. During RL, the teacher head drifts from WBW_{B} by 1.65%1.65\% in relative Frobenius norm. The resulting term (WT−WB)​h~T(W_{T}-W_{B})\tilde{h}_{T} has 50%50\% of the norm of the native logit change, compared with 94%94\% for the representation term, and the two have cosine similarity −0.23-0.23. Fixed-head and native-head targets differ by 18.70%18.70\% in mean relative logit error, although the corresponding distributions have a mean KL divergence of 0.00580.0058 and a top-11 agreement of 96.90%96.90\%. The representation-space target contains no head-drift term. For the student update in Fig. 5(b), the residual-alignment cosine is 0.9540.954 (prompt-bootstrap 95%95\% CI [0.949,0.958][0.949,0.958]), the head-visible cosine is 0.8950.895 over 5.20×1055.20\times 10^{5} coordinates, and the mean projection along the residual is 1.691.69 (CI [1.65,1.73][1.65,1.73]).

Appendix F Additional Learning-Signal Diagnostics

From each method’s on-policy validation rollouts, we use 143143 problems, 44 rollouts per problem, and 1616 positions per rollout drawn uniformly from the last 2,0002{,}000 response tokens, giving 9,1529{,}152 fixed prefixes per method. For ExOPD, summing over the full vocabulary of 151,936151{,}936 tokens at each prefix gives the exact conditional moments Var⁡[ℓ]\mathrm{Var}[\ell], Var⁡[ρ]\mathrm{Var}[\rho], and Cov⁡[ℓ,ρ]\mathrm{Cov}[\ell,\rho], and hence Varv∼p​[Aλ]\mathrm{Var}_{v\sim p}[A_{\lambda}] for any λ\lambda. Resampling the next token 8,1928{,}192 times per prefix reproduces the exact values to within 0.38%0.38\%. For RIDE, we measure ‖∇hℒλ‖2\|\nabla_{h}\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}\|_{2} at each fixed prefix and resample the next token 8,1928{,}192 times per prefix (7.50×1077.50\times 10^{7} draws in total, with adjacent draws differing in 19.50%19.50\% of cases).

Averaged over prefixes, the ExOPD conditional variance follows Eq. 9 with fitted coefficients

Var⁡[Aλ]= 0.0096− 0.0421​(λ−1)+ 0.153​(λ−1)2.\mathrm{Var}[A_{\lambda}]\;=\;0.0096\;-\;0.0421\,(\lambda-1)\;+\;0.153\,(\lambda-1)^{2}.

The terms are Var⁡[ℓ]=0.0096\mathrm{Var}[\ell]=0.0096, −2​Cov​[ℓ,ρ]=−0.0421-2\,\mathrm{Cov}[\ell,\rho]=-0.0421, and Var⁡[ρ]=0.153\mathrm{Var}[\rho]=0.153. The negative covariance term produces a minimum of 0.00670.0067 at λ≈1.14\lambda\approx 1.14; beyond this point the quadratic term dominates, giving 2.80×2.80\times the λ=1\lambda=1 variance at λ=1.50\lambda=1.50 and 12.60×12.60\times at λ=2\lambda=2 (0.1210.121 versus 0.00960.0096; prompt-bootstrap 95%95\% CIs [0.101,0.146][0.101,0.146] and [0.0084,0.0111][0.0084,0.0111], respectively). In Fig. 5c, shading shows these confidence intervals and the dashed curve isolates (λ−1)2​Var​[ρ](\lambda-1)^{2}\,\mathrm{Var}[\rho], which accounts for essentially all growth beyond λ≈1.30\lambda\approx 1.30.

For RIDE, the target h⋆h^{\star} depends on the prefix and the frozen models but not on the token drawn next. The variance of its per-position gradient norm across resampled tokens is therefore exactly zero at every prefix and every λ\lambda; the red curve is placed at the plotting floor and does not represent a measured positive value. The gradient norm does vary across prefixes (between-prefix variance ≈4×103\approx 4\times 10^{3} at every λ\lambda), which reflects variation in the data rather than next-token sampling noise.

Appendix G Implementation and Diagnostics

Training and evaluation configuration.

Table 5 lists the configuration shared by all methods; only the target construction differs between runs. Final answers are extracted with the standard boxed parser and graded by exact match. Table 6 summarizes the per-rollout cost of each method relative to OPRD: RIDE adds one frozen forward pass of πB\pi_{B} on the teacher worker and no additional communication, since h⋆h^{\star} is formed in place and a single hidden-state tensor is transmitted, as for OPRD.

Target construction.

The frozen pre-RL checkpoint is loaded into the worker that already hosts the teacher. For each rollout, this worker runs one additional forward pass of πB\pi_{B}, forms h⋆h^{\star} in place according to Eq. 6, and transmits a single hidden-state tensor to the trainer, so the transfer volume equals that of OPRD. The loss, layer alignment, and position mask are those of OPRD; positions outside the mask or beyond the response length are zero-padded in both hidden-state tensors, so h⋆h^{\star} vanishes there and the masked loss is unaffected. When λ=1\lambda=1 or no base checkpoint is provided, the base model is neither loaded nor evaluated, and training coincides with OPRD.

Remark G.1 (Loss scale).

At initialization the student coincides with the base, hθ0=hBh_{\theta_{0}}=h_{B}, so hθ0−h⋆=−λ​Δh_{\theta_{0}}-h^{\star}=-\lambda\Delta and the initial per-position loss is λ2​‖Δ‖22/d\lambda^{2}\|\Delta\|_{2}^{2}/d, a factor λ2\lambda^{2} larger than for OPRD. Because Eq. 4 is unnormalized, changing λ\lambda therefore also changes the effective step size. We keep the unnormalized form so that λ=1\lambda=1 recovers OPRD exactly, and multiply the loss coefficient by λ−2\lambda^{-2}, which equalizes the initial loss with that of OPRD for every λ\lambda; loss values at different λ\lambda are compared after this rescaling.

Diagnostics.

During training we log the cosine similarity between hBh_{B} and hTh_{T}, the residual norm ratio ‖Δ‖2/‖hT‖2\|\Delta\|_{2}/\|h_{T}\|_{2} both overall and per layer, and the target norm ratio ‖h⋆‖2/‖hT‖2\|h^{\star}\|_{2}/\|h_{T}\|_{2}, which directly monitors the scale sensitivity described in Remark G.1.
